facts.text: UN regulations are shared road-vehicle approval rules written at the United Nations in Geneva: UN R131 and UN R152 address emergency braking on trucks and cars, UN R159 addresses moving-off information, and UN R171 addresses driver assistance. WP.29, GRVA, VMAD and NATM are respectively the forum, working party, expert group and method that produce these rules.
facts.quote: The UN regulations are the shared road-vehicle approval rules written at the United Nations in Geneva, R131 and R152 for emergency braking on trucks and cars, R159 for moving-off information and R171 for driver assistance

facts.text: Most countries outside North America approve road vehicles against regulations agreed at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE).
facts.quote: Most countries outside North America approve road vehicles against regulations agreed at the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe (UNECE).

entities.name: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe

facts.text: WP.29, the World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations, adopts UNECE vehicle regulations; GRVA is its working party on automated, autonomous and connected vehicles.
facts.quote: The forum that adopts them is WP.29, the World Forum for Harmonization of Vehicle Regulations; its working party on automated, autonomous and connected vehicles is GRVA

facts.text: VMAD (Validation Method for Automated Driving), an informal group under GRVA, developed the New Assessment/Test Method (NATM).
facts.quote: an informal group under it, VMAD (Validation Method for Automated Driving), developed the New Assessment/Test Method (NATM)

facts.text: UNECE road-vehicle bodies do not regulate a quarry loader or haul truck; the booklet classifies all evidence from these bodies as on-road evidence.
facts.quote: All are road-vehicle bodies, and the booklet marks everything from them as "on-road evidence" that does not regulate a quarry loader or haul truck

entities.name: United Nations Economic Commission for Europe

facts.text: UN R131 covers advanced emergency braking on heavy vehicles, and its 02 series entered into force on 4 January 2023.
facts.quote: UN R131 covers advanced emergency braking on heavy vehicles. Its 02 series, in force 4 January 2023

facts.text: UN R131's 02 series requires a warning at least 0.8 seconds before emergency braking.
facts.quote: requires a warning at least 0.8 s before emergency braking

facts.text: UN R131's 02 series requires a braking demand of at least 4 m/s² and tabulated impact speeds.
facts.quote: a braking demand of at least 4 m/s², tabulated impact speeds

facts.text: UN R131's 02 series requires a child pedestrian target conforming to ISO 19206-2.
facts.quote: a child pedestrian target to ISO 19206-2

facts.text: UN R131's 02 series requires a false-reaction test between two parked cars 4.5 metres apart at 50 km/h.
facts.quote: a false-reaction test between two parked cars 4.5 m apart at 50 km/h

facts.text: UN R131's 02 series permits no more than 10 percent failed runs in robustness testing.
facts.quote: no more than 10 percent failed runs in robustness testing

facts.text: UN R152 covers cars and vans, with car-to-car tests at 10–60 km/h and pedestrian tests at 20–60 km/h.
facts.quote: UN R152 covers cars and vans, with car-to-car tests at 10 to 60 km/h and pedestrian tests at 20 to 60 km/h

facts.text: UN R152 supplements adopted by WP.29 in 2025 permit virtual testing as an alternative to some physical tests; the manufacturer and authority agree the number of physical confirmation tests.
facts.quote: supplements adopted by WP.29 in 2025 permit virtual testing as an alternative to some physical tests, with the number of physical confirmation tests "defined in agreement between" manufacturer and authority

facts.text: A January 2024 GRVA paper found an earlier UN R152 virtual-testing proposal short of the full credibility framework.
facts.quote: after a January 2024 GRVA paper found an earlier proposal short of the full credibility framework

facts.text: UN R159 (2021) covers moving-off information systems that warn truck drivers about pedestrians and cyclists in front of the truck.
facts.quote: UN R159 (2021) covers moving-off information systems that warn truck drivers of pedestrians and cyclists in front

facts.text: The booklet cites UN R159's small-cylinder visibility method and road users moving at 3–5 km/h.
facts.quote: the booklet cites its small-cylinder visibility method and road users moving at 3 to 5 km/h

facts.text: UN R171 (2025) covers driver control assistance systems and permits validation to include virtual testing.
facts.quote: UN R171 (2025) covers driver control assistance systems: validation "may include the use of virtual testing"

facts.text: When virtual testing is used under UN R171, an Annex 5 credibility assessment must be provided to the Type Approval Authority; the manufacturer must demonstrate the tool's scope, validity for the scenario and toolchain validation.
facts.quote: "a credibility assessment as described in Annex 5 shall be provided to the Type Approval Authority", with the manufacturer demonstrating the tool's scope, its validity for the scenario and the toolchain's validation

facts.text: NATM has five pillars: audit and assessment, virtual testing, track testing, real-world testing and in-service monitoring.
facts.quote: NATM has five pillars (audit and assessment, virtual testing, track testing, real-world testing, in-service monitoring)

facts.text: NATM's credibility framework covers toolchain management, analysis, verification, validation and uncertainty.
facts.quote: a credibility framework covering toolchain management, analysis, verification, validation and uncertainty

facts.text: NATM requires the outcome of the credibility assessment to define the envelope in which the virtual tool can be used.
facts.quote: "the outcome of the credibility assessment will define the envelope in which the virtual tool can be used"

facts.text: The European Union's Implementing Regulation 2022/1426 on automated-vehicle approval includes an annex related to NATM and states that simulation shall not substitute for physical tests.
facts.quote: The European Union's Implementing Regulation 2022/1426 on automated-vehicle approval carries a related annex and states that simulation "shall not be a substitute for physical tests"

facts.text: The booklet concludes that the UN road-vehicle rules are the most developed rules anywhere for accepting simulation as safety evidence.
facts.quote: These are the most developed rules anywhere for accepting simulation as safety evidence

facts.text: The booklet adopts the structure of the UN road-vehicle simulation rules for off-road validation: qualify the toolchain, state its envelope, retain physical tests as the default and spot-check.
facts.quote: the booklet adopts their structure: qualify the toolchain, state the envelope, keep physical tests as the default and spot-check

facts.text: The content of the UN road-vehicle rules does not transfer to off-road validation because road geometry, car targets, asphalt and the type-approval regime itself are absent off-road.
facts.quote: Their content does not transfer (road geometry, car targets, asphalt and the type-approval regime itself are absent off-road)

facts.text: No off-road body has adopted an equivalent to the UN road-vehicle rules for accepting simulation as safety evidence.
facts.quote: no off-road body has adopted an equivalent

facts.text: The booklet uses on-road false-reaction tests as the model for off-road false-activation tests involving berms, dust plumes and parked machines.
facts.quote: The on-road false-reaction tests are the model for off-road false-activation tests with berms, dust plumes and parked machines
